engRhHs: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets…" — Winston Churchill (1940). Which strategy is used?
Anaphora (repetition at the start of clauses)
Churchill repeats "we shall fight" at the start of each clause to build determination.
"Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country." — John F. Kennedy (1961). Which strategy is used?
Kennedy reverses "you" and "your country" in the second half, which is chiasmus.
"A house divided against itself cannot stand." — Abraham Lincoln (1858), speaking of a nation split over slavery. Which strategy is used?
Lincoln compares the divided nation to a house, without using "like" or "as."
"Is life so dear, or peace so sweet, as to be purchased at the price of chains and slavery?" — Patrick Henry (1775). Which strategy is used?
Henry asks a question he expects no one to answer "yes" to, to make his point.
"Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few." — Winston Churchill (1940). Which strategy is most prominent?
Churchill places the opposites "so many" and "so few" side by side for effect.
"I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat." — Winston Churchill (1940). Which strategy is used?
Churchill lists four vivid images of hardship to prepare listeners for sacrifice.
"With malice toward none, with charity for all…" — Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address (1865). Which strategy is used?
Both phrases follow the pattern "with ___ toward/for ___" while contrasting "none" and "all."
"I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king." — Queen Elizabeth I (1588). Which strategy is used?
Concession followed by a contrasting claim
Elizabeth first grants a perceived weakness, then turns it with "but" to assert her strength.
"Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere." — Martin Luther King Jr. (1963). Which strategy is used?
"Let every nation know… that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe…" — John F. Kennedy (1961). Which strategy is used?
Parallel structure in a series of verb phrases
Each phrase follows the same verb + "any" + noun pattern, building rhythm and resolve.
"Give me liberty, or give me death!" — Patrick Henry (1775). Which strategy is used?
Henry presents only two extreme options to show how much he values liberty.
"We refuse to believe that the bank of justice is bankrupt." — Martin Luther King Jr. (1963), continuing his image of a promissory note. Which strategy is used?
King develops the comparison of America's promises to a cheque across several sentences.
"From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent." — Winston Churchill (1946). Which strategy is used?
Churchill describes the division of Europe as an "iron curtain," a metaphor for a hard barrier.
"Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation…" — Abraham Lincoln (1863). What is the main effect of beginning this way?
It recalls the nation's founding in solemn, formal language
It gives a precise statistic about battles
It tells a humorous personal story
Counting back to 1776 in biblical-sounding language reminds listeners of the founding ideals.
Frederick Douglass asked an 1852 audience, "What, to the American slave, is your Fourth of July?" What was the main purpose of this question?
To expose the hypocrisy of celebrating freedom while slavery existed
To ask for directions to the celebration
To introduce a statistic about July
The question forces listeners to confront the gap between their ideals of liberty and the reality of slavery.
"The only thing we have to fear is fear itself." — Franklin D. Roosevelt (1933), during the Great Depression. What was the main purpose of this line?
To calm a frightened public and discourage panic
To list the causes of the Depression
Roosevelt reframes fear itself as the danger, urging Americans not to give in to panic.
"It was we, the people; not we, the white male citizens; nor yet we, the male citizens; but we, the whole people, who formed the Union." — Susan B. Anthony (1873). Which strategy is used?
Repetition of a famous phrase to redefine it
Anthony repeats "we, the people" from the Constitution to argue it includes women.
"Ich bin ein Berliner" ("I am a Berliner"). — John F. Kennedy, speaking in West Berlin (1963). What strategy does this line mainly use?
Identifying with the audience to show solidarity
Using sarcasm to mock the crowd
Telling a story about his childhood
By declaring himself a Berliner in their language, Kennedy aligns himself with his listeners.
"Never retract, never explain, never apologize — get the thing done and let them howl." — attributed to Nellie McClung. Which strategy is used?
The repeated "never" at the start of each phrase creates a forceful rhythm.
A wartime speaker calls a devastating defeat "a setback of some inconvenience." Which strategy is this?
Describing a devastating loss in mild terms deliberately downplays it.
"Let freedom ring from the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire. Let freedom ring from the mighty mountains of New York." — Martin Luther King Jr. (1963). Which strategy is used?
Anaphora (repetition at the start of sentences)
Each sentence begins with "Let freedom ring," building momentum across the speech's ending.
A nineteenth-century speaker opens, "I speak to you not as a politician, but as a mother who has buried two sons in this war." Which appeal does this mainly establish?
Ethos and pathos through personal experience
Her personal loss gives her credibility and stirs the audience's emotions.

"Lay" means to put something down and takes an object, here "the books."
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
My brother is taller than I am.
My brother is taller then I am.
My brother is more taller than I am.
My brother is taller than me am.
"Than" is used for comparisons, and "I am" completes the clause.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
Jamal and I went to the concert.
Jamal and me went to the concert.
Me and Jamal went to the concert.
Myself and Jamal went to the concert.
"I" is the subject pronoun needed here.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
The coach gave the awards to Ava and me.
The coach gave the awards to Ava and I.
The coach gave the awards to Ava and myself.
The coach gave the awards to I and Ava.
"Me" is the object of the preposition "to."
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
We need a lot of chairs for the event.
We need alot of chairs for the event.
We need allot of chairs for the event.
We need a lots of chairs for the event.
"A lot" is always written as two words.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
I will try to finish the project tonight.
I will try and finish the project tonight.
I will try finishing to the project tonight.
I will tried to finish the project tonight.
Standard formal English uses "try to," not "try and."
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
Being that it was raining, we stayed inside.
Being as how it was raining, we stayed inside.
Because of it was raining, we stayed inside.
"Because" is standard; "being that" is non-standard.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
She feels bad about missing the meeting.
She feels badly about missing the meeting.
She feels badder about missing the meeting.
She feels worstly about missing the meeting.
After a linking verb like "feels," use the adjective "bad."
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
He played well in the final game.
He played good in the final game.
He played gooder in the final game.
He played more good in the final game.
"Well" is the adverb describing how he played.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
Anyway, we should get started.
Anyways, we should get started.
Anywayz, we should get started.
Any ways, we should get started.
"Anyway" is the standard form.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
Supposedly, the bus is coming at noon.
Supposably, the bus is coming at noon.
Supposebly, the bus is coming at noon.
Supposingly, the bus is coming at noon.
"Supposedly" is standard; "supposably" is a common error.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
The two friends divided the pizza between themselves.
The two friends divided the pizza between theirselves.
The two friends divided the pizza between themself.
The two friends divided the pizza between their selves.
"Themselves" is the standard reflexive pronoun.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
Less sugar is better for your teeth.
Fewer sugar is better for your teeth.
Lesser sugar is better for your teeth.
Least sugar is more better for your teeth.
Use "less" with uncountable nouns such as sugar.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
Who did you lend your notes to?
Who did you lend your notes too?
Who did you borrow your notes to?
Who did you loan your notes two?
"Lend" means to give temporarily, and "to" is the correct preposition.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
Can I borrow your calculator?
Can I lend your calculator?
Can I borrow you your calculator?
Can you borrow me your calculator?
You borrow from someone and lend to someone.
Which sentence uses standard English correctly?
The reason for the delay is that the pilot was ill.
The reason for the delay is because the pilot was ill.
The reason why for the delay is because the pilot was ill.
The reason for the delay is due to because the pilot was ill.
"The reason … is that" avoids the redundant "reason … because."
